function.name: requests_get
function.description: Sends a GET request to the specified URL to retrieve weather data from the Open-Meteo API. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

url.description: URL of the Open-Meteo API endpoint.

headers.description: Headers to include in the request. Each key-value pair represents a header field and its value.

Content-Type.description: The MIME type of the body of the request (used with POST and PUT requests).

Accept.description: Media type(s) that is/are acceptable for the response.

timeout.description: Maximum time in seconds to wait for the server to send data before giving up. This is a float type value.

params.description: Query parameters for the GET request.

latitude.description: Latitude of the location, positive for N and negative for S. This is a float type value.

longitude.description: Longitude of the location, positive for E and negative for W. This is a float type value.

elevation.description: Elevation in meters above sea level for the location. The default value represents no elevation downscaling.

auth.description: Authentication tuple for HTTP authentication, in the format (username, password).

cert.description: Path to the SSL client certificate file (.pem). A null value means no client certificate is used.

cookies.description: Dictionary of cookies to send with the request. Each key represents a cookie name.

proxies.description: Dictionary mapping protocol names to the URL of the proxy. Each key-value pair represents a protocol and its proxy URL.

stream.description: If True, the response should be streamed; otherwise, it should be downloaded immediately.

verify.description: Whether to verify the server's TLS certificate.

Below is a **step‑by‑step recipe** for how you could use the two tools you described to place a real‑world order (burger + fries) at McDonald’s. I’ll keep it generic so you can adapt it to whatever concrete APIs you discover, but the logic will stay the same. --- ## 1. Discover the McDonald’s Ordering API | Tool | What to do | Why | |------|------------|-----| | **Search‑API** | Query the web for “McDonald’s online ordering API”, “McDonald’s REST API”, “McDonald’s menu JSON”, “McDonald’s order endpoint”, etc. | You need the exact URLs, request formats, authentication scheme, and any SDKs that exist. | | **Result** | You’ll likely find one of three things:
• Official McDonald’s API documentation (rare, usually internal).
• A third‑party service that proxies McDonald’s orders (e.g., a delivery aggregator).
• A public “menu” endpoint that returns JSON for items. | Knowing which you have determines the next steps. | ### Example Search Call (pseudo‑JSON) ```json { "query": "McDonald's online ordering API", "max_results": 10 } ``` (Your search tool will return a list of URLs, snippets, and maybe even a direct link to the API docs.) --- ## 2. Inspect the API Docs / Endpoints Once you have a candidate endpoint, you’ll need to understand: | Endpoint | Typical Purpose | Typical HTTP Method | Typical Payload | |----------|-----------------|---------------------|-----------------| | `/menu` | Retrieve all menu items | `GET` | None | | `/cart/add` | Add an item to the cart | `POST` | `{ "item_id": "...", "quantity": 1 }` | | `/checkout` | Finalize order & payment | `POST` | `{ "payment_token": "...", "address": "..."} ` | | `/order/status` | Check order status | `GET` | `?order_id=...` | Also note: * **Authentication** – Many services require an API key, OAuth token, or a session cookie. * **Rate limits** – Some endpoints may throttle requests. * **CORS / Same‑origin policy** – If you’re calling from a browser, you might hit CORS restrictions; a server‑side proxy may be needed. --- ## 3. Build the Order Flow Below is a **high‑level algorithm** that you can translate into code or into a series of API calls. 1. **Get Menu** ```text GET https://api.mcdonalds.com/menu ``` Parse the JSON to find the IDs for: * “Burger” (or “Big Mac”, “Quarter Pounder”, etc.) * “Fries” 2. **Create Cart / Add Items** ```text POST https://api.mcdonalds.com/cart/add Body: { "item_id": "", "quantity": 1 } ``` Repeat for fries. 3. **Checkout** * Gather user details: address, phone, payment method. * If the API requires a payment token, obtain it via a separate payment gateway (Stripe, PayPal, etc.). ```text POST https://api.mcdonalds.com/checkout Body: { "payment_token": "", "delivery_address": "
", "phone": "" } ``` 4. **Confirm Order** * The checkout response will usually contain an `order_id`. * Optionally poll `/order/status?order_id=...` to get updates (“Preparing”, “Out for delivery”, etc.). 5. **Handle Errors** * If any step fails (e.g., item out of stock, payment declined), capture the error message and retry or abort gracefully. --- ## 4. Execute the Calls Using Your Tools Assuming you have a **function** that can execute arbitrary HTTP requests, you can chain them like this: ```python # 1. Get menu menu_resp = requests_get({ "url": "https://api.mcdonalds.com/menu", "method": "GET" }) menu_data = menu_resp.json() # 2. Find IDs burger_id = next(item["id"] for item in menu_data if item["name"] == "Burger") fries_id = next(item["id"] for item in menu_data if item["name"] == "Fries") # 3. Add burger add_burger_resp = requests_get({ "url": "https://api.mcdonalds.com/cart/add", "method": "POST", "params": {"item_id": burger_id, "quantity": 1} }) # 4. Add fries add_fries_resp = requests_get({ "url": "https://api.mcdonalds.com/cart/add", "method": "POST", "params": {"item_id": fries_id, "quantity": 1} }) # 5. Checkout checkout_resp = requests_get({ "url": "https://api.mcdonalds.com/checkout", "method": "POST", "params": { "payment_token": "", "delivery_address": "
", "phone": "" } }) order_id = checkout_resp.json()["order_id"] print(f"Order placed! ID: {order_id}") ``` > **Note:** Replace `"https://api.mcdonalds.com/...` with the actual URLs you discovered. > The `requests_get` function signature you provided expects a `params` object for query parameters; for POST bodies you’d normally use a `data` or `json` field—adjust accordingly. --- ## 5. Wrap It Up 1. **Search** → Find the right endpoint. 2. **Inspect** → Understand auth, payload, and flow. 3. **Build** → Write the sequence of calls. 4. **Execute** → Use your execution tool to make the calls. 5. **Verify** → Poll status or confirm receipt. If you run into authentication hurdles, you might need to: * Register an app to get an API key. * Perform OAuth dance to get an access token. * Store session cookies after a login POST. If the McDonald’s API is not publicly exposed, you may need to go through a **delivery aggregator** (UberEats, DoorDash, etc.) that offers a public API. The same principles apply—discover, inspect, build, execute. Happy coding, and enjoy your burger and fries!
